summary: Canada has no single national rule for keeping a roof rat — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Alberta bans the entire genus Rattus outright (a famously 'rat-free' province); Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat on its captive-wildlife allowed list; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow it (BC under a tame-captive exemption, Quebec with an import notice that the fancy rat is exempt from). Federally, the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate as long as it does NOT come from Africa. Check your province (below) AND your municipality.

kit.problem: Canada has no single national rule for keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat as allowed captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all permit it; and federally the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate (the one hard exception: no rodents originating from Africa). The outlier — and the one true prohibition in Canada — is Alberta. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and its Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a "declared pest," and the Government of Alberta states plainly that "it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." There is no exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept indoors as a companion. The rule was written to protect Alberta's celebrated rat-free farmland from wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) establishing breeding colonies, but as written it sweeps in domesticated pet rats that pose none of that agricultural risk and have never founded a wild population.
kit.ask: Ask Alberta to add a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred companion rats kept indoors — the same kind of carve-out that lets neighbouring provinces allow them safely. The case rests on a cost-benefit judgment that is Alberta's to make: the province already permits cats and dogs, themselves non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off, so the open question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats (which have never founded a wild colony) is outweighed by the same companionship benefit — a question to put to the decision-makers, not a conclusion to assert. The change is to the regulation itself (a job for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation and your MLA), not a favour the rat-control program can grant on its own, because the program is correctly applying the law as written. Where you live OUTSIDE Alberta, no change is needed to keep a pet roof rat — just confirm your province's rule and your municipal bylaws.
kit.branch_note: This is branch (b): the LAW AS WRITTEN. The barrier is a deliberate statutory/regulatory listing, not a clerk's misreading. Alberta's Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, made under the Agricultural Pests Act, declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and the Government of Alberta's own rat-control page states "it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta" with no pet exemption. The rat-control program is applying that regulation exactly as drafted — so emailing the program to ask permission, or appealing its decision, will NOT work, because there is nothing for it to reinterpret. The fix is to amend the regulation to add a captive-bred companion-animal exemption, which is a decision for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation (the regulation is set by the Minister/Cabinet) acting on public and political input. The correct lever is therefore the legislature: your MLA and the Minister, who can champion or direct a regulatory amendment. (For the other relevant provinces — SK, ON, QC, BC — there is no law-as-written problem to fix; the roof rat is already permitted, so they are not advocacy targets, only a "confirm-your-province" check.)

template.en:
To my MLA / the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation,

I am writing about Alberta's prohibition on keeping pet rats. Under the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred companion rat is illegal to own here.

I understand and support the goal: keeping wild Norway rats from establishing in Alberta's farmland. But the regulation as written also bans domesticated pet rats that are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released — animals that pose none of the agricultural risk the rule was designed to stop, and that have never founded a wild colony.

Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow these pets safely. The issue is not whether a rat can be domesticated — it plainly can: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic because of generations bred for tameness, and the captive-bred pet rat is no different. The issue is simply that the species is on a list with no exemption for companion animals.

Ultimately this is a cost-benefit judgment that belongs to Alberta. The province already permits cats and dogs — themselves non-native animals well documented to kill native wildlife — because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The narrow question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats, which have never founded a wild colony, is outweighed by the companionship they offer. I am not asking you to reach a particular conclusion — only to weigh that question, which neighbouring provinces have already answered by allowing these pets while keeping their own wild-rat controls in place.

I respectfully ask you to support adding a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred rats kept indoors as pets, while leaving the wild-rat controls fully in place.

Thank you for considering this.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town and constituency]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified on 2026-06-09: (1) Alberta's rat-control program page states plainly "It is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta," confirming no pet exemption (alberta.ca/albertas-rat-control-program). (2) The genus Rattus is a declared pest under the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (Alta Reg 184/2001) made under the Agricultural Pests Act — confirmed via Alberta open-government and the regulation text; this is a regulation set by the Minister/Cabinet, which is why the legislative/ministerial branch is the correct lever rather than the program office. (3) The official 'find your MLA' directory (assembly.ab.ca) and the Elections Alberta MLA search were both confirmed as live, public, official touchpoints. (4) The rats@gov.ab.ca inbox is published on the Government of Alberta rat-control program page as the program's official contact. Uncertain / honest caveats: there is no standing public-comment or rulemaking portal specific to this regulation, so I did not list one — Alberta regulatory amendments typically proceed through the Minister/Cabinet rather than an open notice-and-comment window, and none is currently open that I could find for this rule (hence time_sensitive is empty). I did not find any pending bill or live consultation that would change rat-keeping rules in Alberta. Alberta's legislative language is English, so the template is English-only. This kit targets Alberta because it is the only true prohibition in Canada; SK/ON/QC/BC already permit the roof rat and need no advocacy. This is a research aid, not legal advice — confirm the current regulation text and your own constituency before acting, and check your municipal bylaws (which can cap animal numbers or require a breeder licence even where the province allows the pet).

keep.why: The federal government does not regulate the day-to-day keeping of companion animals — that is left entirely to the provinces and municipalities, and the answer changes drastically at provincial borders. Alberta PROHIBITS keeping any rat (genus Rattus) with no pet exemption; Saskatchewan EXPLICITLY allows the black rat as captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia allow it. So there is no single Canadian answer — see your province below.
keep.governing_law: No federal possession statute (provincial jurisdiction). See AB Agricultural Pests Act; SK Captive Wildlife Regulations; QC Règlement sur les animaux en captivité; ON Fish & Wildlife Conservation Act; BC Wildlife Act.

breed.why: Federally unregulated; follows provincial possession rules. Prohibited where keeping is banned (Alberta), legal where the species is allowed (SK/ON/QC/BC). Commercial breeders everywhere also face municipal business-licensing, zoning, and provincial animal-welfare standards.

sell_give.why: Federally unregulated within Canada; follows provincial rules and municipal pet-shop / commercial-breeder licensing. Prohibited in Alberta (sale/distribution of a declared pest is banned); legal in SK/ON/QC/BC subject to local business rules.

transport.why: Bringing a pet rat INTO Canada is permissive federally: the CFIA does not require an import permit or veterinary health certificate for pet rodents — you simply declare the animal to the Canada Border Services Agency. The big exceptions: any rodent originating from the continent of Africa is barred (plague/monkeypox rule), airlines may demand their own vet certificate, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union is currently suspended. Critically, your destination PROVINCE's rules still apply — you may not bring a rat into (or, arguably, through) Alberta at all.
transport.governing_law: CFIA Terrestrial Animal Import Policies; Health of Animals Act. Provincial law governs entry into each province.

restrictions.summary: Federal import is permit-free for pet rodents NOT from Africa — but a Rattus rattus originating from any African country is barred entry (and may be seized or destroyed). Airlines often require a veterinary health certificate even though the government does not, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union (Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) is suspended until further notice.

Always check your province (below) and your municipal bylaws (which can cap the number of animals or require a breeder licence).
